Idiom (Kabiye): Ɛyʋ́ ɛhʋmɩŋ nɛ hʋ́nʋ́ʋ́, taahʋ́mɩ-na taɣtáɣ.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Binary conditional construction: an affirmative protasis followed by a negative imperative/apodosis; fixed proverbial clause with instrumental phrases.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Do not repay kindness or restraint with cruelty. A response should be proportionate and humane, even when one has the power to retaliate.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Paɣ hɛɛ nɛ ɛyʋ́ weyi paɣ-ŋ hɛɛ; taaɣzɩɣ tɔm ɛzaɣtʋ.
Usage Contexts: Family mediation; conflict resolution; advice to young people; community justice; reconciliation.
Register and Tone: Traditional, admonitory, morally serious; occasionally ironic when someone overreacts.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Recorded in proverb research from the Kara Kabiye-speaking area. The contrast between hʋ́nʋ́ʋ́ ‘razor’ and the older word taɣtáɣ ‘potsherd’ encodes proportionality and humane reciprocity.
First Example Sentence: Wiyaʋ se: «Ɛyʋ́ ɛhʋmɩŋ nɛ hʋ́nʋ́ʋ́, taahʋ́mɩ-na taɣtáɣ.»
Second Example Sentence: Ñɩma ɛkɛ́yɛ tɔm ɛzaɣtʋ, Pɩyɛ́ɣa ɖɩ se: «Ɛyʋ́ ɛhʋmɩŋ nɛ hʋ́nʋ́ʋ́, taahʋ́mɩ-na taɣtáɣ.»
Third Example Sentence: Ɛlɛ ɛyʋ́ laɣzɩ́ɣ-ŋ, taaɣzɩɣ-ɩ; «Ɛyʋ́ ɛhʋmɩŋ nɛ hʋ́nʋ́ʋ́, taahʋ́mɩ-na taɣtáɣ.»

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Two coordinated perfective clauses with contrasting animal subjects; compact binary proverb.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A stronger or more powerful actor may seize what a weaker actor has obtained. Success is not secure until it is protected.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Ɛyʋ́ paɣá tɔm, ɛlɛ ɛyʋ́ paɣlaa mʋ́-ɩ.
Usage Contexts: Politics; workplace rivalry; trade; inheritance disputes; humorous commentary on unequal power.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Draws on raptor imagery familiar in rural Kabiye ecological knowledge. The older lexical item makɩyɛ ‘falcon’ is noted as less familiar among younger urban speakers.
First Example Sentence: Kpeluú kpáɣá nɛ makɩyɛ mʋ́; tɔm pɩ́ɣ hɛɛ.
Second Example Sentence: Ɛyʋ́ kpáɣá pɩyɛ, ɛlɛ ɛyʋ́ paɣlaa mʋ́-ɩ: «Kpeluú kpáɣá nɛ makɩyɛ mʋ́.»
Third Example Sentence: Wiyaʋ pɔ́zʋ́ʋ se: «Kpeluú kpáɣá nɛ makɩyɛ mʋ́» nɛ tɩ́ɣ tɔm nɩ́ɩ.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Negative reciprocal clause: plural human subject + negative imperfective verb + reciprocal object phrase.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: People who depend on one another should not sabotage each other’s means of livelihood or mutual support.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Avatɩnáa paɣ hɛɛ ɖamá; taaɣzɩɣ ɖamá tɔm.
Usage Contexts: Mutual aid; farming groups; market associations; family obligations; cooperative work.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Based on the older rural institution of petitioners or mutual-help seekers carrying baskets. The proverb preserves avatɩnáa, a word reported as becoming obsolete among younger speakers in Kara.
First Example Sentence: Avatɩnáa ɛɛlɔ́ʋ ɖamá ɖaakúlá; ɖamá tɔm kɛ́na hɛɛ.
Second Example Sentence: Tɔmɩyɛ nɛ sɔɔlɩm lábʋ́ ɖamá, «Avatɩnáa ɛɛlɔ́ʋ ɖamá ɖaakúlá.»
Third Example Sentence: Ɛyáa pɩ́yɛ ɖamá tɔm, wiyaʋ se: «Avatɩnáa ɛɛlɔ́ʋ ɖamá ɖaakúlá.»

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Equative possessive clause: human referent + body-part noun + copular/equative marker + possessed relational noun.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Material needs and hunger strongly influence loyalty and friendship; people often support those who feed or sustain them.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Ɛyʋ́ pɩ́yɛ́ɣa ɛyʋ́ weyi háɣ́na-ɩ pʊyɔɔ.
Usage Contexts: Daily speech; hospitality; politics; patronage; family provision; humorous criticism.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Reflects the central role of food-sharing and hospitality in Kabiye social relations. The older noun ceu ‘friend’ is documented as increasingly unfamiliar to younger speakers.
First Example Sentence: Ɛyʋ lótu lɛ́ ɛ-ceu; háɣ́na pʊyɔɔ nɛ tɔm leleŋ.
Second Example Sentence: Yaa háɣ́na-ŋ pʊyɔɔ, nɛ ɛyʋ́ se: «Ɛyʋ lótu lɛ́ ɛ-ceu.»
Third Example Sentence: Tɔmɩyɛ pɔ́zʋ́ʋ ɖamá, ɛlɛ wiyaʋ sɛ́ɣ se: «Ɛyʋ lótu lɛ́ ɛ-ceu.»

Idiom (Kabiye): Tɔ́m leleŋ ñɔ́ɔ́zɩɣ, tɔ́m ɛzaɣtʋ wɛɛkɩɣ.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Balanced binary assertion with parallel noun phrases and opposed verbs: ‘gentle speech repairs; bad speech destroys.’
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Kind words reconcile people, whereas harsh words damage relationships and institutions.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Tɔ́m hɛɛ paɣ tɔm hɛɛ; tɔ́m ɛzaɣtʋ paɣ tɔm ɛzaɣtʋ.
Usage Contexts: Family counseling; leadership; education; workplace communication; dispute settlement.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: An established Kabiye proverb organized through lexical opposition between ñɔ́ɔ́zɩɣ ‘repair/arrange’ and wɛɛkɩɣ ‘destroy,’ illustrating the rhythmic binary form emphasized in Kabiye proverbial style.
First Example Sentence: Tɔ́m leleŋ ñɔ́ɔ́zɩɣ, tɔ́m ɛzaɣtʋ wɛɛkɩɣ; paɣ tɔ́m hɛɛ.
Second Example Sentence: Halʋ́ se nɛ ɛyáa: «Tɔ́m leleŋ ñɔ́ɔ́zɩɣ, tɔ́m ɛzaɣtʋ wɛɛkɩɣ.»
Third Example Sentence: Wiyaʋ hʋʋ tɔm nɛ lɩmaɣzá, nɛ pɩse: «Tɔ́m leleŋ ñɔ́ɔ́zɩɣ, tɔ́m ɛzaɣtʋ wɛɛkɩɣ.»

Idiom (Kabiye): Tɛtʋ wɛɛ ɖóŋ ɛlɛ́ canzɩ́ ɖɔŋ hɛɛ hɛɛ.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Adversative binary clause: stative description followed by a contrasting habitual-motion clause with an ideophonic adverbial repetition.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Patience and steady effort can overcome severe difficulty.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Paɣ tɔm hɛɛ hɛɛ; taaɣzɩɣ nɛ fɛndu.
Usage Contexts: Farming; education; long projects; healing; encouragement; personal development.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Uses the hard earth and the slow-moving chameleon, both familiar features of Kabiye rural life, to teach persistence. The reduplicated hɛɛ hɛɛ adds rhythm and depicts gradual movement.
Phonetic Transcription (IPA, Kabiye): /tɛ.tʊ wɛː ɖóŋ ɛ.lɛ́ t͡ʃan.zɪ́ ɖɔŋ hɛː hɛː/
First Example Sentence: Tɛtʋ wɛɛ ɖóŋ ɛlɛ́ canzɩ́ ɖɔŋ hɛɛ hɛɛ; taaɣá.
Second Example Sentence: Ɛyʋ́ ɛwɛɛ tɔm ɖóŋ yɔ, wiyaʋ se: «Tɛtʋ wɛɛ ɖóŋ ɛlɛ́ canzɩ́ ɖɔŋ hɛɛ hɛɛ.»
Third Example Sentence: Súkúlibυa paɣ tɔm hɛɛ hɛɛ nɛ pɩlɛ́ɣ: «Tɛtʋ wɛɛ ɖóŋ ɛlɛ́ canzɩ́ ɖɔŋ hɛɛ hɛɛ.»

Idiom (Kabiye): Efeleu ɛfɛyɩ ña-ɖɩɣa taá, agbaa taá tʋ eehikiɣ-ŋ.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Conditional negative construction with locative contrast ‘inside/outside’; complex fixed sentence with a causal inference.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: External enemies usually succeed only when someone inside betrays or assists them.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Ɛyʋ́ agbaa eehikiɣ-ŋ ɛlɛ ɛyʋ́ ɖɩɣa taá paɣ-ɩ.
Usage Contexts: Politics; family disputes; security; workplace confidentiality; warnings about betrayal.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Draws on traditional beliefs about sorcery while encoding a broader social lesson about insider betrayal. The house contrasts symbolically with the outside world.
Phonetic Transcription (IPA, Kabiye): /e.fe.le.u ɛ.fɛ.jɪ ɲa.ɖɪ.ɣa táː, a.gbaː táː tʊ eː.hi.kɪɣ ŋ/
First Example Sentence: Efeleu ɛfɛyɩ ña-ɖɩɣa taá, agbaa taá tʋ eehikiɣ-ŋ; pɔ́zʋ́ʋ ña-ɖamá.
Second Example Sentence: Wiyaʋ tɛ́tʋ se: «Efeleu ɛfɛyɩ ña-ɖɩɣa taá, agbaa taá tʋ eehikiɣ-ŋ.»
Third Example Sentence: Tɔm ɛzaɣtʋ kɔ́ɔ ɖɩɣa taá yɔ, ɖoɖo se: «Efeleu ɛfɛyɩ ña-ɖɩɣa taá, agbaa taá tʋ eehikiɣ-ŋ.»

Idiom (Kabiye): Ɛgɔm ɛsá paɣláa ɛlɛ aanáɣ políŋ.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Adversative coordinated clause: possessed body-part subject + adjective, followed by a negative perception predicate.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A newcomer may observe many things but lacks the deep local knowledge needed to foresee consequences.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Ɛgɔm aanáɣ tɔm políŋ; ɛyʋ́ ɖɩɣa taá nɩ́ɩ tɔm.
Usage Contexts: Migration; village affairs; workplace onboarding; politics; advice to visitors.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Rooted in Kabiye attitudes toward situated knowledge: large eyes symbolize visible attention, but distance symbolizes historical and social understanding unavailable to a newcomer.
First Example Sentence: Ɛgɔm ɛsá paɣláa ɛlɛ aanáɣ políŋ; pɔ́zʋ́ʋ tɔm.
Second Example Sentence: Ɛgɔm kɔ́ɔ tɛ́tʋ yɔ, wiyaʋ se: «Ɛgɔm ɛsá paɣláa ɛlɛ aanáɣ políŋ.»
Third Example Sentence: Tɔmɩyɛ pɩ́yɛ ɛgɔm tɔm nɛ pɩse: «Ɛgɔm ɛsá paɣláa ɛlɛ aanáɣ políŋ.»

Idiom (Kabiye): Ɛyáa naálɛ káɣ́ pɩ́yɛ nɛ pókúlí-ɖɩ́.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Plural human subject with numeral, reciprocal/united action predicate, and purposive action phrase.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Cooperation makes difficult work possible; unity creates strength.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Ɛyáa paɣ tɔm ɖamá yɔ, pɩ́yɛ tɔm ɖóŋ.
Usage Contexts: Community labor; farming; school teamwork; family projects; associations; public mobilization.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Evokes collective agricultural labor: two people combine effort to uproot a stone. It reflects cooperative work traditions in Kabiye communities.
First Example Sentence: Ɛyáa naálɛ káɣ́ pɩ́yɛ nɛ pókúlí-ɖɩ́; ɖamá kɛ́na ɖóŋ.
Second Example Sentence: Cíca se nɛ súkúlibυa: «Ɛyáa naálɛ káɣ́ pɩ́yɛ nɛ pókúlí-ɖɩ́.»
Third Example Sentence: Haɖύ pɩ́yɛ tɔm ɖamá nɛ pɩlɛ́ɣ: «Ɛyáa naálɛ káɣ́ pɩ́yɛ nɛ pókúlí-ɖɩ́.»

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Simple gnomic assertion: body-part subject + habitual verb + related body-part object.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: One should respect elders, leaders, protectors, and legitimate authority.
Usage Contexts: Family etiquette; chieftaincy; initiation; education; workplace hierarchy; public ceremonies.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Uses the anatomical relation between the eye and eyelid to model social hierarchy and protection. The image links respect with interdependence rather than mere submission.
First Example Sentence: Ɛsɩ́yɛ ñaŋ ɛsɩhuɖuu; paɣ sɩ́yɛ nɛ wiyaʋ.
Second Example Sentence: Ɖoɖo se nɛ sukulibυa: «Ɛsɩ́yɛ ñaŋ ɛsɩhuɖuu.»
Third Example Sentence: Kamʋ́ taá, ɛyáa paɣ sɩ́yɛ nɛ pɩse: «Ɛsɩ́yɛ ñaŋ ɛsɩhuɖuu.»
